title: Dyslipidaemia and Atherosclerotic Risk
sourceTitle: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification
edition: NG238, published 14 December 2023; recommendations retrieved 12 October 2026
scope: Adults being assessed for primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease; this limited extraction covers formal risk assessment, lipid and secondary-cause testing, selected statin decisions and monitoring.
gaps: QRISK3 was developed for a UK population and must be reconciled with current Saudi cardiovascular-risk policy and population calibration. NICE supports atorvastatin 20 mg in defined groups but the recommendation text does not provide a complete route, frequency, duration, interaction and contraindication set, so no medication regimen is encoded. Pregnancy contraindication is recorded, but all current product information, liver, muscle, interaction and intolerance checks remain mandatory. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: What is the estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk in an adult without established cardiovascular disease?
investigations.finding: NICE recommends QRISK3 for people aged 25 to 84 without CVD and prioritises full assessment when estimated 10-year risk is 10% or more.
investigations.rationale: Formal risk assessment supports shared decisions on preventive treatment while recognising that risk may be underestimated in some people.
investigations.timeframe: At preventive assessment; review estimates on an ongoing basis for people over 40

investigations.test: Full lipid profile and secondary-cause assessment
investigations.question: What is the lipid pattern and is a secondary or familial disorder plausible?
investigations.finding: Measure total, HDL, non-HDL and triglyceride values and assess alcohol use, diabetes, thyroid disease, liver disease and nephrotic syndrome; use family history and findings to assess familial disease.
investigations.rationale: Secondary causes and familial dyslipidaemia alter treatment and referral.
investigations.timeframe: Before lipid-lowering treatment

investigations.question: Is statin treatment safe and achieving the expected lipid response?
investigations.finding: Baseline assessment includes diabetes status, renal function and transaminases; repeat full lipid profile and transaminases 2 to 3 months after starting or changing treatment, and transaminases at 12 months.
investigations.rationale: Monitoring checks response and identifies clinically important adverse effects.
investigations.timeframe: Baseline, 2 to 3 months after starting or changing treatment, and transaminases at 12 months

actions.instruction: Use shared decision-making after lifestyle and modifiable-risk review; NICE recommends atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention when 10-year QRISK3 is 10% or more and allows consideration below that threshold when risk may be underestimated or the person prefers treatment.
Do not use statins during pregnancy; stop if pregnancy is possible, stop 3 months before attempting conception and do not restart until breastfeeding is finished.

title: Elective Cholecystectomy Pre-operative Assessment Pathway
sourceTitle: Routine preoperative tests for elective surgery
locator: Recommendations 1.1 to 1.7 and Tables 1 to 3 for minor, intermediate and major or complex surgery by ASA grade
scope: Adults over 16 preparing for elective non-cardiothoracic surgery; this limited extraction applies the NICE preoperative-test framework to elective cholecystectomy after the local team assigns procedure grade and ASA class.
gaps: NICE NG45 is a 2016 UK testing guideline and does not replace a cholecystectomy-specific history, examination, imaging review, indication check, anaesthetic assessment, bile-duct evaluation, thrombosis plan or current Saudi perioperative protocol. Laparoscopic versus open procedure grade must be assigned locally. No antimicrobial, analgesic, anticoagulant or other medicine regimen is verified. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.test: Procedure grade and ASA physical-status assessment
investigations.question: Which NICE testing table applies to the planned procedure and the person's comorbidity burden?
investigations.finding: NICE selects routine tests by minor, intermediate or major/complex surgery and ASA grade rather than ordering a universal panel.
investigations.rationale: Test need changes with surgical magnitude and systemic disease.
investigations.timeframe: At preoperative assessment before ordering tests

investigations.test: Full blood count, kidney function and resting ECG as indicated
investigations.question: Which tests are supported by the assigned surgery and ASA category?
investigations.finding: Use the NICE tables: requirements range from not routine to consider or offer according to surgery grade, ASA status and cardiovascular, renal or diabetes comorbidity.
investigations.rationale: The table-based approach reduces unnecessary testing while detecting abnormalities likely to alter perioperative care.
investigations.timeframe: During preoperative assessment, using recent valid results when appropriate

investigations.question: Is recent glycaemic assessment available for a person with diabetes?
investigations.finding: Include the latest HbA1c in the referral and offer testing if it has not been measured in the previous 3 months; do not routinely test people without diagnosed diabetes.
investigations.rationale: Recent glycaemic status informs perioperative planning without screening every surgical patient.
investigations.timeframe: Within 3 months before surgery for people with diabetes

actions.instruction: Carry forward relevant test results already obtained in primary care and avoid duplicating valid investigations.
actions.timeframe: At surgical referral and preoperative review

actions.instruction: If anticoagulant treatment needs modification, create an individualised perioperative plan using current local guidance; routine coagulation tests do not measure direct oral anticoagulant effect.

title: Elective Coronary Revascularisation Review
edition: CG126, published 23 July 2011; last updated 25 August 2016
scope: Adults with stable angina being considered for elective coronary revascularisation; this limited extraction covers persistent symptoms, coronary anatomy, functional assessment, multidisciplinary review and CABG versus PCI decisions.
gaps: This older UK guideline requires reconciliation with current ESC, ACC/AHA and Saudi revascularisation guidance, contemporary physiology and intravascular-imaging practice, stent technology, diabetes evidence and surgical-risk tools. It does not verify antiplatelet, anticoagulant, antianginal, lipid-lowering or peri-procedural regimens. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Are stable-angina symptoms satisfactorily controlled and is the diagnosis still secure?
investigations.finding: Persistent symptoms despite optimal medical treatment are a NICE indication to consider revascularisation.
investigations.rationale: Revascularisation for stable angina is selected in relation to symptom burden, treatment response and prognostic anatomy.
investigations.timeframe: Before invasive strategy selection

investigations.test: Coronary angiography with functional assessment when required
investigations.question: What is the coronary anatomy and does a lesion explain clinically important ischaemia?
investigations.finding: NICE recommends coronary angiography to guide strategy when symptoms remain uncontrolled; additional non-invasive or invasive functional testing may be required.
investigations.rationale: Anatomy and functional significance guide whether CABG, PCI or continued medical treatment is appropriate.
investigations.timeframe: Before revascularisation decision

investigations.test: Systematic anatomic and clinical complexity assessment
investigations.question: Do left-main, proximal three-vessel or complex multivessel disease and comorbidities favour CABG or PCI?
investigations.finding: Assess coronary severity and complexity with diabetes, age, comorbidities and procedural suitability.
investigations.rationale: NICE identifies potential CABG survival advantage in selected multivessel disease and requires individual risk-benefit comparison.
investigations.timeframe: At multidisciplinary review

actions.instruction: Discuss complex anatomy, left-main disease, anatomically complex three-vessel disease or uncertain strategy in a team including cardiac surgeons and interventional cardiologists.

Give balanced information on continued medical treatment, CABG and PCI, including symptom relief, procedural risks, repeat-revascularisation likelihood and possible survival advantage in selected disease.

title: Elective Hernia Repair Assessment
sourceTitle: Update of the international HerniaSurge guidelines for groin hernia management
locator: Updated statements and recommendations in Chapters 6a-b, 6d, 6f, 7 and 8; sections on mesh versus non-mesh repair, approach selection and occult contralateral hernia
scope: Adults with groin hernia being assessed for elective repair; this limited extraction covers symptom and hernia-characteristic review, shared decisions on repair approach, mesh considerations and watchful-waiting evidence for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic men.
gaps: This international society update supplements rather than replaces the 2018 HerniaSurge guideline and is focused on selected updated questions. It does not establish a complete preoperative test panel or cover all ventral, incisional, paediatric, strangulated or obstructed hernias. Current Saudi surgical pathways, surgeon expertise, female femoral-hernia risk, anaesthetic assessment and local device governance require reconciliation. No medicine regimen is verified. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.test: Structured hernia history and physical examination
investigations.question: Are symptoms, reducibility, functional impact, acute warning features and prior repairs defined?
investigations.finding: Assessment should distinguish elective groin hernia from acutely symptomatic disease and document patient and hernia characteristics that influence approach.
investigations.rationale: Urgency and repair method depend on symptoms, anatomy, prior surgery and patient factors.
investigations.timeframe: At surgical assessment

investigations.test: Assessment for occult or contralateral groin hernia
investigations.question: Is there a clinically occult contralateral hernia and would identifying it change the agreed plan?
investigations.finding: Occult contralateral hernia management has uncertain natural history and should be addressed through informed discussion rather than automatic repair.
investigations.rationale: Repair can prevent later surgery but exposes an asymptomatic side to procedural risk.
investigations.timeframe: Before or during minimally invasive repair planning

investigations.test: Patient and hernia suitability for mesh, non-mesh, open or laparo-endoscopic repair
investigations.question: Which approach best fits anatomy, infection risk, preferences and available expertise?
investigations.finding: Mesh repair is recommended for most adults because recurrence is lower; selected people may choose non-mesh repair when expertise is available, and infection can contraindicate permanent mesh.
investigations.rationale: Technique selection balances recurrence, pain, rare mesh complications and surgeon competence.
investigations.timeframe: Before listing and consent

actions.instruction: Use shared decision-making to explain mesh and non-mesh options, recurrence, chronic pain, sexual symptoms, rare visceral complications and the experience of the operating team.
For asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in men, discuss watchful waiting as an option while explaining that many people later cross over to surgery because of symptoms.

title: Elective Hip and Knee Arthroplasty Preparation
sourceTitle: Joint replacement (primary): hip, knee and shoulder
locator: Recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.4 and 1.2.1; sections on shared decision-making, information and preoperative rehabilitation
scope: Adults offered primary elective hip or knee replacement; this limited extraction covers shared decisions, preparation information and preoperative rehabilitation.
gaps: This UK guideline must be reconciled with current Saudi arthroplasty pathways, implant governance, blood management, venous-thromboembolism prevention, infection prevention, anaesthetic assessment, dental policy and local rehabilitation capacity. It is not a complete surgical eligibility or optimisation protocol and no medicine regimen is verified. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Does the person understand alternatives, likely benefits, procedural risks, implant choices and possible future surgery?
investigations.finding: NICE requires procedure-specific information and discussion of alternatives, anaesthesia, analgesia, recovery and rehabilitation.
investigations.rationale: Expectations, preferences and informed consent shape whether and how joint replacement proceeds.
investigations.timeframe: From the first surgical appointment and throughout preparation

investigations.question: Which exercise, functional, lifestyle or support needs could affect recovery?
investigations.finding: Assess exercise capacity, independence, weight-management needs, diet, smoking and barriers to postoperative rehabilitation.
investigations.rationale: Preoperative advice prepares the person for surgery and engagement in recovery.
investigations.timeframe: When listed for hip or knee replacement

actions.instruction: Give advice on exercises to perform before and after surgery, lifestyle measures including weight management, diet and smoking cessation, and maximising functional independence and quality of life.
Provide clear information on hospital stay, pain, wound care, rehabilitation, return to work and return to usual activities, with a contact route for questions.
actions.timeframe: Before surgery and reinforced as needed

title: Elective Hysterectomy for Benign Disease
sourceTitle: Heavy menstrual bleeding: assessment and management
edition: NG88, published 14 March 2018; last updated 7 July 2026
locator: Recommendations 1.2.6, 1.3.3 to 1.3.11, 1.4.4 and 1.4.7 to 1.4.9, plus route and oophorectomy recommendations
scope: Women with heavy menstrual bleeding considering elective hysterectomy for benign disease; this limited extraction covers anaemia assessment, uterine-cavity investigation, endometrial sampling when indicated and informed surgical decisions.
gaps: This pathway is limited to heavy menstrual bleeding and does not cover every benign hysterectomy indication, suspected cancer, prolapse, endometriosis or acute bleeding. It requires reconciliation with Saudi gynaecology pathways, cervical screening, pregnancy exclusion, anaesthetic assessment, thrombosis prevention and local consent standards. Pretreatment medicines are mentioned by NICE but no complete regimen or contraindication set is verified here. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Is anaemia or another blood-count abnormality present in a woman with heavy menstrual bleeding?
investigations.finding: NICE recommends a full blood count for all women with heavy menstrual bleeding in parallel with treatment.
investigations.rationale: Blood loss and anaemia affect symptoms, optimisation and surgical planning.
investigations.timeframe: During initial assessment and before surgery when clinically required

investigations.test: Outpatient hysteroscopy or pelvic ultrasound selected from history and examination
investigations.question: Is a submucosal fibroid, polyp, endometrial pathology, adenomyosis or larger fibroid suspected?
investigations.finding: Use outpatient hysteroscopy when cavity pathology is suspected and ultrasound when examination or symptoms indicate larger fibroids, a mass or adenomyosis.
investigations.rationale: Identifying structural disease informs whether hysterectomy and which route are appropriate.
investigations.timeframe: Before definitive surgical planning

investigations.test: Endometrial biopsy at hysteroscopy when high risk
investigations.question: Is there increased risk of endometrial pathology?
investigations.finding: Consider biopsy during diagnostic hysteroscopy for high-risk women; do not perform blind endometrial biopsy for heavy menstrual bleeding.
investigations.rationale: Targeted sampling improves diagnostic context and avoids unsupported blind sampling.
investigations.timeframe: At diagnostic hysteroscopy when risk criteria are present

actions.instruction: Discuss fertility loss, sexual function, bladder function, alternatives, complications, psychological impact, expectations and the possible need for further treatment before deciding on hysterectomy.
Individualise vaginal, laparoscopic or abdominal route and total versus subtotal hysterectomy; remove ovaries only with the woman's express informed consent after discussing risks and benefits.

title: Elective Valve Intervention Assessment
sourceTitle: Heart valve disease presenting in adults: investigation and management
edition: NG208, published 17 November 2021; reviewed 24 October 2025 with a TAVI update in development
scope: Adults with suspected or confirmed heart valve disease being assessed for elective intervention; this limited extraction covers echocardiography, urgent features, severity markers, surveillance and intervention selection.
gaps: NICE states that its TAVI recommendations are under review, creating a current-edition conflict that must be reconciled before approval. This UK guidance also requires Saudi Heart Team policy, local surgical-risk assessment, CT planning, coronary assessment, frailty, life expectancy, pregnancy and prosthesis-anticoagulation pathways. No medicine or antithrombotic regimen is verified. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Is valve disease present and how severe is it?
investigations.finding: Offer echocardiography when a suspicious murmur is accompanied by symptoms, signs or an abnormal ECG, and use it to quantify valve lesion, ventricular response and intervention thresholds.
investigations.rationale: Valve anatomy and haemodynamic severity drive specialist referral and timing.
investigations.timeframe: At diagnostic assessment; urgently when high-risk symptoms are present

investigations.test: Urgent specialist assessment for high-risk symptoms
investigations.question: Are exertional syncope, severe breathlessness or angina likely related to valve disease?
investigations.finding: A systolic murmur with exertional syncope warrants specialist assessment including echocardiography within 2 weeks; severe symptoms also warrant urgent assessment.
investigations.rationale: These features can indicate severe disease with elevated short-term risk.
investigations.timeframe: Within 2 weeks

investigations.question: Do symptoms, valve severity, ventricular function, exercise testing, natriuretic peptides or CT findings indicate intervention?
investigations.finding: NICE uses lesion-specific echo thresholds and, for selected aortic stenosis, exercise testing, BNP or NT-proBNP, dobutamine stress echo, calcium score and cardiac MRI.
investigations.rationale: Multimodal assessment identifies asymptomatic people whose risk may justify intervention and clarifies uncertain severity.
investigations.timeframe: Before Heart Team decision

actions.instruction: Offer intervention to adults with symptomatic severe valve disease and select surgery, transcatheter intervention or conservative management through shared specialist assessment.

For asymptomatic severe valve disease suitable for intervention but without a current indication, provide clinical review with echocardiography every 6 to 12 months, adjusted to findings and shared decisions.

title: Fetal Growth Restriction Assessment
sourceTitle: Investigation and Care of a Small-for-Gestational-Age Fetus and a Growth Restricted Fetus
edition: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 31, third edition, first published 13 May 2024; correction/update noted July 2026
locator: Official RCOG landing page and linked full-text key recommendations; risk assessment by 14 weeks, uterine artery Doppler, serial biometry, umbilical artery Doppler and birth-timing recommendations
scope: Singleton pregnancies at low, moderate or high risk of a small-for-gestational-age fetus or fetal growth restriction; multiple pregnancy and fetal anomaly are outside the source scope.
gaps: The July 2026 correction warns against Intergrowth-21 estimated-fetal-weight charts in the NHS population; chart selection must be reconciled with Saudi population validation and local maternity policy. Aspirin 150 mg nightly from 12+0 to 36+0 weeks is supported for women at risk of pre-eclampsia or placental dysfunction, but the linked recommendation does not state route or a complete contraindication and interaction set, so no medication regimen is encoded. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Does maternal medical, obstetric or current-pregnancy history require enhanced surveillance?
investigations.finding: RCOG recommends assessment at booking by 14 weeks and updating risk after the anomaly scan and throughout pregnancy.
investigations.rationale: Early risk classification determines whether fundal-height surveillance, uterine artery Doppler or serial ultrasound is needed.
investigations.timeframe: By 14 weeks, after the mid-trimester scan and whenever risk changes

investigations.test: Uterine artery Doppler for high-risk pregnancy
investigations.question: Is there evidence of increased placental resistance?
investigations.finding: For high-risk women, perform uterine artery Doppler between 18+0 and 23+6 weeks; abnormal mean pulsatility index above the 95th centile leads to earlier serial growth scans.
investigations.rationale: Placental Doppler stratifies surveillance timing for growth disorders.
investigations.timeframe: 18+0 to 23+6 weeks

investigations.test: Serial fetal biometry and umbilical artery Doppler
investigations.question: Is fetal size or growth trajectory abnormal and is there placental compromise?
investigations.finding: Once SGA is identified, repeat biometry every 2 weeks and perform umbilical artery Doppler at diagnosis and at least every 2 weeks.
investigations.rationale: Serial size, growth velocity and Doppler distinguish constitutional smallness from fetal growth restriction and guide birth timing.
investigations.timeframe: At diagnosis and at least every 2 weeks

actions.instruction: For women at risk of pre-eclampsia or placental dysfunction, the RCOG recommendation is aspirin 150 mg once daily at night from 12+0 to 36+0 weeks; confirm route, contraindications, interactions and local policy before prescribing.

Escalate early FGR before 32 weeks to tertiary multidisciplinary fetal-medicine and neonatal care; base birth timing on gestation, Doppler, growth, CTG, maternal condition and the guideline's lesion-specific recommendations.
actions.timeframe: At diagnosis and with any deterioration

title: Gestational Diabetes Identification and Management Pathway
sourceTitle: Diabetes in pregnancy: management from preconception to the postnatal period
edition: NG3, published 25 February 2015; last updated 16 December 2020
scope: Pregnant women being assessed for or diagnosed with gestational diabetes; this limited extraction covers risk-based OGTT, diagnostic thresholds, early review, glucose targets and treatment escalation.
gaps: This older UK recommendation uses NICE diagnostic thresholds that may differ from WHO, IADPSG or current Saudi pathways. It must be reconciled with Saudi antenatal screening strategy, laboratory standards and medicine formulary. Metformin and insulin are named, but exact product, dose, route, frequency, titration, duration and complete contraindications are not supplied in the selected recommendations, so no medication regimen is encoded. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Is risk-based diagnostic testing indicated?
investigations.finding: At booking, assess BMI 30 kg/m² or above, previous baby 4.5 kg or above, previous gestational diabetes, first-degree family history and high-prevalence ethnicity.
investigations.rationale: NICE uses these factors to select women for diagnostic testing.
investigations.timeframe: At the booking appointment

investigations.question: Does the woman meet NICE criteria for gestational diabetes?
investigations.finding: Diagnose if fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or above or the 2-hour value is 7.8 mmol/L or above.
investigations.rationale: The OGTT and specified thresholds establish diagnosis in the source pathway.
investigations.timeframe: At 24 to 28 weeks for risk factors; earlier after booking for previous gestational diabetes, repeating at 24 to 28 weeks if initially normal

investigations.question: Are individualised pregnancy glucose targets being met without problematic hypoglycaemia?
investigations.finding: NICE targets are fasting below 5.3 mmol/L, 1-hour post-meal below 7.8 mmol/L or 2-hour post-meal below 6.4 mmol/L; insulin-treated women should stay above 4 mmol/L.
investigations.rationale: Frequent glucose data guide escalation and reduce maternal and fetal risk.
investigations.timeframe: Daily after diagnosis according to treatment regimen

actions.instruction: Arrange review in a joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week of diagnosis and refer to a dietitian.

If fasting glucose is below 7.0 mmol/L at diagnosis, offer diet and exercise initially; if targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks, offer metformin, or insulin if metformin is contraindicated or unacceptable.
If fasting glucose is 7.0 mmol/L or above at diagnosis, offer immediate insulin with or without metformin plus diet and exercise changes.

title: Heart Failure
sourceTitle: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management
edition: NG106, published 12 September 2018; last updated 3 September 2025
scope: Adults with suspected or established chronic heart failure; this limited extraction covers NT-proBNP referral thresholds, echocardiography, phenotype classification and selected pre-treatment safety checks.
gaps: This UK guideline requires reconciliation with current Saudi heart-failure pathways, local natriuretic-peptide assays and access to specialist care. NICE names core HFrEF medicine classes and newer HFmrEF/HFpEF options but does not provide a complete product-specific dose, route, frequency, titration, duration and contraindication set in the selected recommendations, so no medication regimen is encoded. Acute decompensated heart failure is outside scope. Existing inherited sections are not newly verified.

investigations.question: Does suspected chronic heart failure require urgent or routine specialist assessment?
investigations.finding: More than 2,000 ng/L warrants specialist assessment and transthoracic echocardiography within 2 weeks; 400 to 2,000 ng/L warrants both within 6 weeks; below 400 ng/L in an untreated person makes heart failure less likely.
investigations.rationale: Natriuretic-peptide level supports referral urgency and identifies when alternative causes should be reviewed.
investigations.timeframe: At initial assessment; referral within 2 or 6 weeks according to result

investigations.question: Is there valve disease, systolic or diastolic dysfunction or an intracardiac shunt?
investigations.finding: Echocardiography defines structural disease and ventricular phenotype for specialist diagnosis and treatment.
investigations.rationale: Treatment differs for reduced, mildly reduced and preserved ejection fraction and for valve disease.
investigations.timeframe: Within the NT-proBNP-directed referral window

investigations.question: Is bradycardia, heart block or another rhythm or conduction abnormality present?
investigations.finding: Assess rhythm, rate and conduction before prescribing; do not offer a beta-blocker for heart rate below 50 beats/minute or second- or third-degree heart block without a pacemaker.
investigations.rationale: Baseline conduction assessment identifies a source-defined contraindication to beta-blocker use.
investigations.timeframe: Before beta-blocker initiation and after dose increments when symptomatic bradycardia requires review

actions.instruction: Refer newly diagnosed, recently decompensated or advanced heart failure to the specialist multidisciplinary team for diagnosis and treatment optimisation.

For HFrEF, NICE recommends an ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist and SGLT2 inhibitor, introduced and monitored according to the source and product-specific guidance; do not use this limited draft as a prescribing protocol.
actions.timeframe: After specialist phenotype and safety assessment
